exampleAnswers.title: Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function

question.text:
Let $F(x) = \sin x$ for $x\in\mathbb R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x \in [0,2\pi)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $f(x+2\pi) = f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  2. $f(x) = F(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  3. $f\left(x+\pi\right) = f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
question.explanation:
Since $f$ is the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have

  • $f(x+2\pi)=f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R},$ and

  • $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x \in [0,2\pi).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $2\pi$-periodicity: \[ f(x+2\pi)=f(x) \] for all $x\in\mathbb{R}.$

  • Statement II is true. Notice that $F$ itself is $2\pi$-periodic, because for any $x\in\mathbb{R},$ we have \begin{align*} F(x+2\pi) = \sin(x+2\pi) = \sin(x) = F(x). \end{align*} Since $F$ already satisfies the periodicity rule, the $2\pi$-periodic extension agrees with $F$ everywhere, so $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}.$

  • Statement III is false. For example, take $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ Then, \begin{align*} f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}+\pi\right)=f\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right)=F\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right)=-1, \end{align*} while \begin{align*} f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=F\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=1. \end{align*}

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

example.title: Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function

question.text:
Let $F(x) = 2x$ for $x\in\mathbb R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $3$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,3)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $f(x+6) = f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  2. $f(x) = F(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  3. $f(x+2) = f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
question.explanation:
Since $f$ is the $3$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have

  • $f(x+3)=f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R},$ and

  • $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x \in [0,3).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. We have \begin{align*} f(x+6) = f\big((x+3)+3\big) = f(x+3) = f(x) \end{align*} for all $x \in \mathbb{R}.$

  • Statement II is false. For example, take $x=4.$ Then, \begin{align*} f(4) = f(1+3) = f(1) = F(1) = 2(1) = 2, \end{align*} while \begin{align*} F(4) = 2(4) = 8. \end{align*} Hence, $f(x) \neq F(x)$ for $x=4.$

  • Statement III is false. For example, take $x=2.$ Then, \begin{align*} f(2+2) = f(4) = f(1+3) = f(1) = F(1) = 2(1) = 2 \end{align*} while \begin{align*} f(2) = F(2) = 2(2) = 4. \end{align*} Hence, $f(x+2) \neq f(2)$ for $x=2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

example.title: Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function

question.text:
Let $F(x) = 4x-1$ for $x\in\mathbb R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $6$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,6)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $f(x+12) = f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  2. $f(x) = F(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  3. $f(x+3) = f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
question.explanation:
Since $f$ is the $6$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have

  • $f(x+6)=f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R},$ and

  • $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x \in [0,6).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. We have \begin{align*} f(x+12)=f\big((x+6)+6\big)=f(x+6) = f(x). \end{align*} for all $x \in \mathbb{R}.$

  • Statement II is false. For example, take $x=7.$ Then, \begin{align*} f(7)=f(1+6)=f(1)=F(1)=3, \end{align*} while \begin{align*} F(7)=27. \end{align*} Hence, $f(x) \neq F(x)$ for $x=7.$

  • Statement III is false. For example, take $x=2.$ Then, \begin{align*} f(2+3)=f(5)=F(5)=19 \end{align*} while \begin{align*} f(2)=F(2)=7. \end{align*} Hence, $f(x+3) \neq f(x)$ for $x = 2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

example.title: Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function

question.text:
Let $F(x) = \sin(x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $\pi$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x \in [0,\pi)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $f(x+\pi) = f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  2. $f(x) = F(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  3. $f(x) = f(x-2\pi)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
question.explanation:
Since $f$ is the $\pi$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have

  • $f(x+\pi)=f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R},$ and

  • $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in[0,\pi).$

With that in mind, we examine each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $\pi$-periodicity: \[ f(x+\pi)=f(x) \] for all $x\in\mathbb{R}.$

  • Statement II is false. For example, take $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}.$ Then, \begin{align*} f\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}+\pi\right) = f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = F\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 1, \end{align*} while \begin{align*} F\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = \sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = -1. \end{align*} Hence, $f(x)\neq F(x)$ for $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}.$

  • Statement III is true. We have \begin{align*} f(x) &= f\big((x-\pi)+\pi\big) \\[5pt] &= f(x-\pi) \\[5pt] &= f((x-2\pi) + \pi) \\[5pt] &= f(x-2\pi) \end{align*} for all $x \in \mathbb{R}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

example.title: Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function

question.text:
Let $F(x) = \sin(2x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $\dfrac{\pi}2$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x \in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}2\right)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}2\right) = f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  2. $f(x) = F(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  3. $f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = f\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
question.explanation:
Since $f$ is the $\pi/2$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have

  • $f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}2\right)=f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R},$ and

  • $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).$

With that in mind, we examine each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $\dfrac{\pi}2$-periodicity: \[ f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}2\right)=f(x) \] for all $x\in\mathbb{R}.$

  • Statement II is false. For example, take $x=\dfrac{3\pi}4.$ Using the periodicity of $f(x):$ \begin{align*} f\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = F\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \sin\left(2 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 1, \end{align*} while \begin{align*} F\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = \sin\left(2 \cdot \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = \sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = -1. \end{align*} Hence, $f(x) \neq F(x)$ for $x= \dfrac{3\pi}{4}.$

  • Statement III is true. Since $f$ is $\dfrac{\pi}2$-periodic, any shift by a multiple of its period returns the same value: \begin{align*} f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = f(x) \quad \text{and} \quad f\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = f\left(\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}2\right)+\dfrac{\pi}2\right) = f(x). \end{align*} Since both sides equal $f(x),$ the statement is true for all $x\in\mathbb{R}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

exampleAnswers.title: Checking Orthogonality of Sines and Cosines

question.text: \[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x) g(x) \, \textrm{d}x \] Given the inner product on the set of continuous functions over $x\in [-\pi,\pi]$ defined above, select the correct options below.
question.explanation:
Evaluating the inner product, we obtain \begin{align*} \langle \cos(5x), 1 \rangle &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \cos(5x)\,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{1}{5}\sin(5x) \right]_{-\pi}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5}\big(\sin(5\pi)-\sin(-5\pi)\big) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5}(0-0) \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{0}. \end{align*}

Therefore, $f(x)=\cos(5x)$ and $g(x)=1$ $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{are orthogonal}}$ with respect to the inner product.

example.title: Checking Orthogonality of Sines and Cosines

question.text: \[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi} f(x) g(x) \, \textrm{d}x \] Given the inner product on the set of continuous functions over $x\in [0,2\pi)$ defined above, select the correct options below.
question.explanation:
We begin by using the product-to-sum identity \[ \sin(3x)\cos(4x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\big(\sin(7x)-\sin(x)\big). \]

Substituting this into the integral gives \begin{align*} \langle \sin(3x), \cos(4x) \rangle &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \sin(3x)\cos(4x)\,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \dfrac{1}{2}\sin(7x)-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin(x) \:\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ -\dfrac{1}{14}\cos(7x)+\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(x) \right]_{0}^{2\pi} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{14}\big(\cos(14\pi)-\cos(0)\big)+\dfrac{1}{2}\big(\cos(2\pi)-\cos(0)\big) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{14}(1-1)+\dfrac{1}{2}(1-1) \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{0}. \end{align*}

Therefore, $f(x)=\sin(3x)$ and $g(x)=\cos(4x)$ $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{are orthogonal}}$ with respect to the inner product.

example.title: Checking Orthogonality of Sines and Cosines

question.text: \[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi} f(x) g(x) \, \textrm{d}x \] Given the inner product on the set of continuous functions over $x\in [0,2\pi]$ defined above, select the correct options below.
question.explanation:
Evaluating the inner product, we obtain \begin{align*} \langle \sin(4x), 1 \rangle &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin(4x)\,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ -\dfrac{1}{4} \cos(4x) \right]_{0}^{2\pi} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{4} (\cos(8\pi) - (\cos(0)) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{4} (1 - 1) \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{0}. \end{align*}

Therefore, $f(x)=\sin(4x)$ and $g(x)=1$ $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{are orthogonal}}$ with respect to the inner product.

example.title: Checking Orthogonality of Sines and Cosines

question.text: \[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x) g(x) \, \textrm{d}x \] Given the inner product on the set of continuous functions over $x\in [-\pi,\pi)$ defined above, select the correct options below.
question.explanation:
We begin by using the product-to-sum identity \[ \sin(4x)\cos(3x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\big(\sin(7x)+\sin(1x)\big). \]

Substituting this into the integral gives \begin{align*} \langle \sin(4x), \cos(3x) \rangle &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin(4x)\cos(3x)\,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \dfrac{1}{2}\sin(7x)+\dfrac{1}{2}\sin(x)\,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ -\dfrac{1}{14}\cos(7x)-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(x) \right]_{-\pi}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{14}\big(\cos(7\pi)-\cos(-7\pi)\big) -\dfrac{1}{2}\big(\cos(\pi)-\cos(-\pi)\big) \\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{1}{14}(-1-(-1)) -\dfrac{1}{2}(-1-(-1))\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{0}. \end{align*}

Therefore, $f(x)=\sin(4x)$ and $g(x)=\cos(3x)$ $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{are orthogonal}}$ with respect to the inner product.

example.title: Checking Orthogonality of Sines and Cosines

question.text: \[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x) g(x) \, \textrm{d}x \] Given the inner product on the set of continuous functions over $x\in [-\pi,\pi)$ defined above, select the correct options below.
question.explanation:
We begin by using the product-to-sum identity \[ \sin(2x)\cos(5x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\big(\sin(7x)-\sin(3x)\big). \]

Substituting this into the integral gives \begin{align*} \langle \sin(2x), \cos(5x) \rangle &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin(2x)\cos(5x)\,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \dfrac{1}{2}\sin(7x)-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin(3x)\,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ -\dfrac{1}{14}\cos(7x)+\dfrac{1}{6}\cos(3x) \right]_{-\pi}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{14}\big(\cos(7\pi)-\cos(-7\pi)\big) +\dfrac{1}{6}\big(\cos(3\pi)-\cos(-3\pi)\big) \\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{1}{14}(-1-(-1)) +\dfrac{1}{6}(-1-(-1))\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{0}. \end{align*}

Therefore, $f(x)=\sin(2x)$ and $g(x)=\cos(5x)$ $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{are orthogonal}}$ with respect to the inner product.

example.title: Checking Orthogonality of Sines and Cosines

question.text:
Let $F(x) = x^2+9x$ for $x\in\mathbb R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [-\pi,\pi)$ to $x\in \mathbb R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

\[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n \cos(nx) + b_n \sin(nx)\right). \] Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient $a_0$ below, where $\langle \:,\rangle$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[-\pi,\pi).$
question.explanation:
The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [-\pi,\pi)$ is given by \[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x. \]

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [-\pi,\pi),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by \[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left( a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \] where $a_0,$ $a_n,$ and $b_n$ are constants to be determined.

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $1{:}$

\begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), 1 \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), 1 \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2},1 \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle a_n\cos(nx), 1 \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle b_n\sin(nx), 1 \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \dfrac{a_0}{2} \left\langle 1,1 \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n \left\langle \cos(nx), 1 \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_n \left\langle \sin(nx), 1 \right\rangle \end{align*}

Since the functions $ 1, \sin(x), \cos(x), \sin(2x), \cos(2x), \ldots $ are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is \[ \dfrac{a_0}{2} \left\langle 1, 1 \right\rangle. \]

Computing the inner product, we have \begin{align*} \left\langle 1, 1 \right\rangle &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} 1 \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ x \right]_{-\pi}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= 2\pi. \end{align*}

Finally, we obtain that \begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), 1 \right\rangle &= \dfrac{a_0}{2} \left\langle 1, 1 \right\rangle \\[5pt] a_0 &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{2\left\langle f(x), 1 \right\rangle}{\left\langle 1, 1 \right\rangle} }\\[5pt] a_0 &= \dfrac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{1}{\pi} } \cdot \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} (x^2+9x)\,\textrm{d}x}. \end{align*}

question.text:
Let $F(x) = 2x^3$ for $x\in\mathbb R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [0,2\pi)$ to $x\in \mathbb R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

\[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n \cos(nx) + b_n \sin(nx)\right). \] Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient $b_2$ below, where $\langle \:,\rangle$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[0,2\pi).$
question.explanation:
The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi)$ is given by \[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \int_{0}^{2\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x. \]

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by \[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left( a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \] where $a_0,$ $a_n,$ and $b_n$ are constants to be determined.

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\sin(2x){:}$

\begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), \sin(2x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \sin(2x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2},\sin(2x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle a_n\cos(nx), \sin(2x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle b_n\sin(nx), \sin(2x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \dfrac{a_0}{2} \left\langle 1,\sin(2x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n \left\langle \cos(nx), \sin(2x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_n \left\langle \sin(nx), \sin(2x) \right\rangle \end{align*}

Since the functions $ 1, \sin(x), \cos(x), \sin(2x), \cos(2x), \ldots $ are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is \[ b_2 \left\langle \sin(2x), \sin(2x) \right\rangle. \]

Computing the inner product, we have \begin{align*} \left\langle \sin(2x), \sin(2x) \right\rangle &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \sin^2(2x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(4x) \:\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{1}{2} x - \dfrac{1}{8} \sin(4x) \right]_{0}^{2\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} (2\pi - 0) - \dfrac{1}{8} (\sin(8\pi) - \sin(0)) \\[5pt] &= \pi. \end{align*}

Finally, we obtain that \begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), \sin(2x) \right\rangle &= b_2 \left\langle \sin(2x), \sin(2x) \right\rangle \\[5pt] b_2 &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{\left\langle f(x), \sin(2x) \right\rangle}{\left\langle \sin(2x), \sin(2x) \right\rangle} }\\[5pt] b_2 &= \dfrac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi} f(x)\sin(2x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{1}{\pi} } \cdot \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\int_{0}^{2\pi} 2x^3\sin(2x)\,\textrm{d}x}. \end{align*}

question.text:
Let $F(x) = x^2$ for $x\in\mathbb R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [-\pi,\pi)$ to $x\in \mathbb R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

\[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n \cos(nx) + b_n \sin(nx)\right). \] Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient $b_2$ below, where $\langle \:,\rangle$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[-\pi,\pi).$
question.explanation:
The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [-\pi,\pi)$ is given by \[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x. \]

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous over $x\in [-\pi,\pi),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by \[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left( a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \] where $a_0,$ $a_n,$ and $b_n$ are constants to be determined.

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\sin(2x){:}$

\begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), \sin(2x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \sin(2x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2},\sin(2x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle a_n\cos(nx), \sin(2x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle b_n\sin(nx), \sin(2x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \dfrac{a_0}{2} \left\langle 1,\sin(2x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n \left\langle \cos(nx), \sin(2x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_n \left\langle \sin(nx), \sin(2x) \right\rangle \end{align*}

Since the functions $ 1, \sin(x), \cos(x), \sin(2x), \cos(2x), \ldots $ are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is \[ b_2 \left\langle \sin(2x), \sin(2x) \right\rangle. \]

Computing the inner product, we have \begin{align*} \left\langle \sin(2x), \sin(2x) \right\rangle &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin^2(2x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(4x) \:\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{1}{2} x - \dfrac{1}{8} \sin(4x) \right]_{-\pi}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} (\pi - (-\pi)) - \dfrac{1}{8} (\sin(4\pi) - (\sin(-4\pi))) \\[5pt] &= \pi. \end{align*}

Finally, we obtain that \begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), \sin(2x) \right\rangle &= b_2 \left\langle \sin(2x), \sin(2x) \right\rangle \\[5pt] b_2 &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{\left\langle f(x), \sin(2x) \right\rangle}{\left\langle \sin(2x), \sin(2x) \right\rangle} }\\[5pt] b_2 &= \dfrac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(2x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{1}{\pi} } \cdot \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} x^2\sin(2x)\,\textrm{d}x}. \end{align*}

question.text:
Let $F(x) = x^3+5x$ for $x\in\mathbb R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [-\pi,\pi)$ to $x\in \mathbb R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

\[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n \cos(nx) + b_n \sin(nx)\right). \] Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient $a_6$ below, where $\langle \:,\rangle$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[-\pi,\pi).$
question.explanation:
The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [-\pi,\pi)$ is given by \[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x. \]

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous over $x\in [-\pi,\pi),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by \[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left( a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \] where $a_0,$ $a_n,$ and $b_n$ are constants to be determined.

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\cos(6x){:}$

\begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), \cos(6x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \cos(6x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2},\cos(6x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle a_n\cos(nx), \cos(6x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle b_n\sin(nx), \cos(6x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \dfrac{a_0}{2} \left\langle 1,\cos(6x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n \left\langle \cos(nx), \cos(6x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_n \left\langle \sin(nx), \cos(6x) \right\rangle \end{align*}

Since the functions $ 1, \sin(x), \cos(x), \sin(2x), \cos(2x), \ldots $ are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is \[ a_6 \left\langle \cos(6x), \cos(6x) \right\rangle. \]

Computing the inner product, we have \begin{align*} \left\langle \cos(6x), \cos(6x) \right\rangle &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \cos^2(6x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(12x) \:\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{1}{2} x + \dfrac{1}{24} \sin(12x) \right]_{-\pi}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} (\pi - (-\pi)) - \dfrac{1}{24} (\sin(12\pi) - (\sin(-12\pi))) \\[5pt] &= \pi. \end{align*}

Finally, we obtain that \begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), \cos(6x) \right\rangle &= a_6 \left\langle \cos(6x), \cos(6x) \right\rangle \\[5pt] a_6 &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{\left\langle f(x), \cos(6x) \right\rangle}{\left\langle \cos(6x), \cos(6x) \right\rangle} }\\[5pt] a_6 &= \dfrac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos(6x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{1}{\pi} } \cdot \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} (x^3+5x)\cos(6x)\,\textrm{d}x}. \end{align*}

question.text:
Let $F(x) = 2x^4-4x^3$ for $x\in\mathbb R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [0,2\pi)$ to $x\in \mathbb R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

\[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n \cos(nx) + b_n \sin(nx)\right). \] Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient $b_3$ below, where $\langle \:,\rangle$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[0,2\pi).$
question.explanation:
The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi)$ is given by \[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \int_{0}^{2\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x. \]

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by \[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left( a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \] where $a_0,$ $a_n,$ and $b_n$ are constants to be determined.

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\sin(3x){:}$

\begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), \sin(3x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \sin(3x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2},\sin(3x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle a_n\cos(nx), \sin(3x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle b_n\sin(nx), \sin(3x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \dfrac{a_0}{2} \left\langle 1,\sin(3x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n \left\langle \cos(nx), \sin(3x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_n \left\langle \sin(nx), \sin(3x) \right\rangle \end{align*}

Since the functions $ 1, \sin(x), \cos(x), \sin(2x), \cos(2x), \ldots $ are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is \[ b_3 \left\langle \sin(3x), \sin(3x) \right\rangle. \]

Computing the inner product, we have \begin{align*} \left\langle \sin(3x), \sin(3x) \right\rangle &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \sin^2(3x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(6x) \:\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{1}{2} x - \dfrac{1}{12} \sin(6x) \right]_{0}^{2\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} (2\pi - 0) - \dfrac{1}{12} (\sin(12\pi) - \sin(0)) \\[5pt] &= \pi. \end{align*}

Finally, we obtain that \begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), \sin(3x) \right\rangle &= b_3 \left\langle \sin(3x), \sin(3x) \right\rangle \\[5pt] b_3 &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{\left\langle f(x), \sin(3x) \right\rangle}{\left\langle \sin(3x), \sin(3x) \right\rangle} }\\[5pt] b_3 &= \dfrac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi} f(x)\sin(3x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{1}{\pi} } \cdot \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\int_{0}^{2\pi} (2x^4-4x^3)\sin(3x)\,\textrm{d}x}. \end{align*}
